title: Chemical Calculations
seo_title: Secondary 3 Chemistry: Chemical Calculations Worksheets (O-Level 6092 with Answers)
standard_text: Construct and use word, formula and ionic equations; define relative atomic mass and relative molecular mass and calculate Mr and percentage composition; use the mole concept and the Avogadro constant; use the molar gas volume of 24 dm³ at room temperature and pressure; calculate concentrations in mol/dm³ and g/dm³ and solve titration problems; calculate reacting masses and volumes of gases from balanced equations; deduce empirical and molecular formulae; calculate percentage yield and percentage purity (summary of the Singapore-Cambridge O-Level Chemistry 6092 syllabus).
meta_desc: Free Secondary 3 O-Level Chemistry worksheets on chemical calculations: Mr, percentage composition, moles, molar gas volume, concentration, titrations, reacting masses, empirical formulae and percentage yield. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Gas: 24 dm³ per mol. Solution: n = c × V (in dm³).
body_html:
How to think about it

Work in moles, then use the mole ratio from the balanced equation.

  • n = mass ÷ Mr; number of particles = n × 6 × 10²³.
  • Gases at r.t.p.: V (dm³) = n × 24. Solutions: n = c × V, with V in dm³ (cm³ ÷ 1000).
  • Reacting masses: mass → moles → use the equation's ratio → moles → mass or volume.
  • Empirical formula: divide each mass by Ar, then by the smallest. % yield = actual ÷ theoretical × 100%.
Example

Moles in 4.0 g of NaOH (Mr 40)?

4.0 ÷ 40

Answer: 0.10 mol

Example

Volume of 0.25 mol of CO₂ at r.t.p.?

0.25 × 24

Answer: 6.0 dm³

Example

25.0 cm³ of 0.1 mol/dm³ NaOH neutralises 20.0 cm³ of HCl. c(HCl)?

n = 0.0025 mol

0.0025 ÷ 0.0200

Answer: 0.125 mol/dm³

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting to use the mole ratio from the equation.
  • Using a volume in cm³ in n = c × V without dividing by 1000.
  • Calculating % yield as theoretical ÷ actual.
  • Using the mass instead of moles when comparing reactants.

faq.q: How do you calculate the number of moles?
faq.a: For a solid or liquid, divide the mass in grams by Mr. For a gas at r.t.p., divide the volume in dm³ by 24. For a solution, multiply concentration (mol/dm³) by volume (dm³).

faq.q: How do you do a reacting mass calculation?
faq.a: Change the given mass into moles, use the ratio in the balanced equation to find the moles of the other substance, then change back into mass (or volume).

faq.q: How do you find an empirical formula?
faq.a: Divide the mass (or percentage) of each element by its Ar, divide by the smallest answer, and round to the simplest whole-number ratio.
